items.item: work_mem is the base budget per sort/hash operation; several operations, or several concurrent sessions, multiply it
Hash-based operations get work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier (default 2.0), more room than sort

at.step: How hash gets more room than sort

items.item: Sort operations are used for ORDER BY, DISTINCT and merge joins; hash tables for hash joins, hash-based aggregation, memoize nodes and hash-based IN-subquery processing
ExecHashIncreaseNumBatches doubles the batch count to reduce current memory consumption, unless growth has been shut off (growEnabled)

at.step: How a batch actually spills and recombines

items.item: A dedicated skew-bucket path keeps a frequent key's matching tuples in memory instead of letting them spill with the rest of their batch

at.step: Why skew needs its own protection

items.item: The bucket count is only ever grown, never shrunk, once batching starts

expert.by: Claude (single session, written from the syllabus line and the fetched sources before storyboarding; not independent of the builder, so a later owner review should repeat it)

items.item: That the default work_mem's spill measured no slower than staying fully in memory on this workload — a real, repeated measurement, not a plausible-sounding rule of thumb
That it's a severely undersized work_mem, not spilling itself, that measurably costs time here
That hash_mem_multiplier, not just work_mem, is the lever the docs themselves recommend when spilling is a regular occurrence

at.step: How hash gets more room than sort

items.item: That a hash join's batch count tracks the memory budget and doubles per halving at the granularity actually tested, read directly off EXPLAIN rather than inferred from widely-spaced settings
The exact mechanism (ExecHashIncreaseNumBatches) that performs the doubling, and its growEnabled cutoff that stops runaway partitioning
That concurrent sessions each pay their own work_mem budget again — measured directly via combined temp-file size during overlap, not just quoted from the docs

That PostgreSQL's skew protection is real and sourced from its own executor code, but not independently observable through this version's EXPLAIN output — named honestly as a gap rather than faked as measured

at.step: Why skew needs its own protection

items.item: That work_mem is a per-operation budget, not a system-wide or even per-query ceiling
That a sort too big for its budget spills to an external merge sort rather than erroring, read off Sort Method directly
That EXPLAIN's own Sort Method and Batches lines are the direct, sufficient signal for whether and how an operator is spilling — no separate 'spilled' flag exists
Recognizing, from an EXPLAIN snippet alone, whether a given operator is spilling and how
Computing a workload's worst-case real memory footprint from its work_mem setting and its concurrency, not just its single-session budget
